messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia Haddad, a 63-year-old auditor who had spent most of her adult life priding herself on steadiness and precision, traced the start of her difficulties to the day her younger sister died on a hiking trip in a state park. Nadia had not been with her when it happened, but she was the one who arrived after the search team had located her. She remembered being led through scrub and dry grass to a narrow ranger outbuilding where her sister’s belongings had been placed, the door shut behind her while an officer spoke in a low voice. What fixed itself in her mind was the combination of confinement and exposure: the locked room, the smell of dirt and sun-warmed brush still clinging to the clothes, and the unbearable fact of her sister reduced to personal effects and descriptions. Ever since, natural settings that resemble that park, enclosed rooms she cannot easily leave, and anything that brings to mind victims have carried an immediate charge for her.

In the months afterward, those moments did not simply upset her; they seemed to strip away the present. If she was in a conference room with the door closed during an audit meeting, or if a client site was on the edge of wooded property, or if she saw a news story showing a grieving family and a victim’s photograph, the memory arrived all at once, without warning. She did not experience it as “remembering” in any ordinary sense. She was back there with the dry air in her throat, the stale indoor smell, the officer’s voice, and the same terror flooding her body as if the loss were happening again. She had come to believe that her body had become an enemy in this way, launching into danger signals even when she knew, rationally, that she was in an office or at home. That belief made the suddenness of these episodes feel even more ominous to her, and once she started scanning constantly for anything that might set them off, she seemed to notice more of them.

Her work gave these fears a daily stage. As an auditor, Nadia was expected to travel to unfamiliar offices, inspect back rooms, and sit through long meetings in windowless spaces with people she did not know. She now avoided unfamiliar places whenever she could, telling colleagues she preferred remote document review or asking for cases closer to home where she could control the environment. She was certain that if she entered a place she had not already mapped out, she would not be able to judge the danger quickly enough. When she could not avoid going, she stayed on guard from the moment she arrived—tracking exits, noting whether doors locked, glancing repeatedly toward hallways, and remaining keyed up through the entire visit. That watchfulness followed her into the night. Sleep became fragmented, not because of a single recurring dream she described, but because her body would not settle; she lay in bed listening for sounds and waking abruptly, already tense.

Over time, her understanding of what had happened to her hardened into darker conclusions. What frightened her most was not only that her sister had died, but that nothing she did—showing up, asking questions, trying to be composed—had changed anything. She had come to believe she could not stop bad things from happening, and from there it did not feel far to deciding that people, life, even God had proved unreliable. Those beliefs fed directly into the way she lived now. If the world was fundamentally unsafe and she was helpless in it, then staying hyperalert made sense; avoiding unknown places felt less like a symptom than common sense. But living in that state also kept proving to her that she was damaged and unprotected. Each sleepless night, each day spent braced in meetings, seemed to confirm that her body would keep reacting as though danger were present and that she could no longer trust herself to feel safe.

The same beliefs also shaped the way reminders struck her. Seeing a victim’s memorial on the local news or even passing a roadside display of flowers could hit with unusual force because it seemed to place her sister among all the other people the world had failed to protect. On weekends, when friends suggested a botanical garden or an outdoor fundraiser, Nadia often refused before she had fully thought it through; natural surroundings had become charged in her mind, not only with memory but with the conviction that terrible things can happen anywhere and no one can prevent them. The more she lived this way—avoiding, scanning, sleeping poorly—the more easily the full sensory reliving broke through, and each episode left her feeling more helpless and more estranged from the faith and trust she once relied on.

She finally sought help after leaving a client meeting in embarrassment when the conference room door clicked shut and she felt the entire scene rush back so vividly that she could barely breathe or orient herself. She told the therapist she was afraid she was “losing the ability to be in the world,” afraid that her work would narrow until she could no longer do it, and afraid that every reminder of another person’s suffering would keep dragging her back to her sister’s death. What she hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget her sister, but to be able to enter a room, sleep through the night, and walk past reminders of loss without feeling that terror take over her whole body again.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Nadia’s negative beliefs directly lead to or intensify the intrusive trauma memory.
The vignette does not clearly show, within one paragraph, that Nadia’s sense of threat causes or strengthens her negative appraisals or beliefs.
The vignette does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that Nadia’s ongoing sense of threat makes triggers/reminders more likely to be noticed or activated.
